blocks.text:
Read the lessons in order; each objective unlocks the next. After a lesson, practise that domain in learning mode, where every answer is explained. Short mocks have 20 questions in 40 minutes and full mocks match the real exam at 45 questions in 90 minutes.

If you want a placement check, take the first short mock in learning mode before reading anything. Treat the result as a rough signal of where to start, not as a measure of ability.

Readiness in this pack asks for more than 90% on recent mocks, a deliberate margin above the real 80% pass mark. Readiness and mastery are practice signals. They are not predictions of your exam result.
blocks.title: How to use the pack

blocks.text:
Most wrong options are not nonsense. They are good practice put in the wrong place.

1. A generic Scrum or project answer where SAFe has a specific one. Example: 'the sprint review' where SAFe means the System Demo of the whole train.
2. A manager deciding where the team or the role should. Example: a manager reordering the team backlog, which belongs to the Product Owner.
3. The right practice given to the wrong role, event or level. Example: the Release Train Engineer prioritising features, which is Product Management's job.

Every lesson ends with a callout that applies these traps to its topic.

lessons.title: 1 · Adapt and thrive with SAFe
lessons.summary: Why Business Agility matters, the dual operating system and the seven core competencies.

blocks.text:
SAFe starts from a claim about the present: we live in the age of software and digital, and every business is a software business. A bank, a freight company and a hospital all compete on how quickly they can turn an idea into a digitally enabled solution. Enterprises that cannot do this lose to those that can.

Business Agility is SAFe's name for the answer. It is the ability to compete and thrive in the digital age by quickly responding to market changes and emerging opportunities with digitally enabled business solutions. Note what it is not: it is not a team practice and it is not an IT programme. It involves everyone who helps deliver solutions, including leaders, finance, legal and operations.
blocks.title: Thriving in the age of disruption

blocks.text:
Why do successful companies become slow? SAFe borrows the explanation from John Kotter. A company begins as an entrepreneurial network of people working directly for customers. As it grows it adds a hierarchy for efficiency and stability: departments, reporting lines, budgets, policies. The hierarchy is useful, but over time its needs crowd out the network, and the company loses the speed it started with.

SAFe does not ask a company to dismantle its hierarchy. It asks for a second operating system beside it: a network organised around value streams, which gives back speed and adaptability, while the hierarchy keeps providing efficiency and stability. In SAFe the network is made of development value streams, each containing one or more Agile Release Trains.
blocks.title: The dual operating system

blocks.text:
A Lean-Agile organisation is built on seven core competencies: Lean-Agile Leadership, Team and Technical Agility, Agile Product Delivery, Enterprise Solution Delivery, Lean Portfolio Management, Organizational Agility and Continuous Learning Culture. The current glossary renames two of them: Agile Product Delivery is now Product Development Flow, and Enterprise Solution Delivery is now Large Solution Integration and Delivery. Recognise both sets of names.

Progress is measured in three domains. Flow shows how efficiently value moves through the system. Outcomes show whether the solutions deliver business benefit. Competency shows how well the organisation practises what enables agility.
blocks.title: Seven core competencies and three measures

blocks.text: Lean-Agile leadership enables the whole stream.
rows: Market and customer signals reveal a possibility
Lean Portfolio Management funds a minimum viable product
People are organised around the work, in value streams
Teams learn what the customer really needs
The smallest solution that can test the idea is delivered
Evidence decides whether to continue, change or stop
The Continuous Delivery Pipeline delivers on demand
blocks.title: Business Agility Value Stream

blocks.text:
Marrow Retail has 9,000 staff and a three-year queue for new digital products. A consultant proposes removing two layers of management. The chief executive instead keeps the hierarchy for pay, compliance and store operations, and forms a network beside it: one development value stream for online ordering, with two trains. Funding moves from 40 small projects to that value stream. The first MVP, kerbside pickup in ten stores, shows customers want one-hour slots, not same-day delivery, and the portfolio pivots.

The SAFe reading: the hierarchy stayed, the network was added, and evidence from an MVP steered the money.
blocks.title: Worked example: Marrow Retail

blocks.text:
Generic answer: 'Business agility means our teams work in sprints.' SAFe answer: it is an enterprise capability that needs all seven competencies.

Generic answer: 'Flatten the hierarchy.' SAFe answer: keep it, and add a value stream network beside it.

Wrong owner: 'The PMO or the coaches run the transformation.' SAFe answer: leaders lead it, because only they can change the system.
blocks.title: SAFe answer versus generic answer

blocks.text:
Pick an organisation you know. Write down:
1. One thing its hierarchy does well that you would keep.
2. One customer-facing flow of work that crosses at least three departments.
3. Which of the three measures, flow, outcomes or competency, it tracks least.
Then say in one sentence what a value stream organised around the flow in step 2 would change.

lessons.title: 2 · Lean-Agile mindset and SAFe Core Values
lessons.summary: What the mindset combines, the five ideas of Lean thinking and the four Core Values.

blocks.text:
SAFe says agility is a change of mindset before it is a change of practice. The Lean-Agile mindset is the combination of beliefs, assumptions, attitudes and actions of leaders and practitioners who embrace two bodies of thought: Lean thinking and the Agile Manifesto. It also needs a growth mindset, the belief that abilities can be developed, because people have to unlearn habits that once made them successful.

A company can run every event in the framework and still fail if its leaders think in the old way: fixed scope, fixed dates, maximum utilisation, decisions at the top.
blocks.title: The Lean-Agile mindset

rows: Value is defined by the customer, for a specific product
Identify the value stream for each product
See every step needed to deliver it
Build in response to demand, not to keep people busy
Keep improving; there is no finished state
blocks.title: Lean thinking in five ideas

blocks.text: The manifesto states four values. It values individuals and interactions over processes and tools, working software over comprehensive documentation, customer collaboration over contract negotiation, and responding to change over following a plan. The items on the right still have value; the items on the left have more. Exam distractors often reverse a pair.
blocks.title: The Agile Manifesto

blocks.text: Earlier versions listed built-in quality and program execution. The current four are the ones above.
rows: Everyone works toward the same vision and objectives
Connecting strategy to backlogs and stating priorities clearly
Facts are visible, including bad news
Making it safe to report problems and sharing their own
People are valued, developed and trusted
Growing people and involving those who do the work in decisions
Giving time to improve and acting on what Inspect and Adapt finds
blocks.title: The four SAFe Core Values

blocks.text:
At Kestrel Foods every feature is reported green until release week. Two years ago a team lead who reported a delay was removed from the project. The trains have all the events, but the status board is fiction.

Which Core Value is missing? Transparency. Alignment may be fine: everyone may agree on the goal. Respect for people is damaged too, but the direct gap is that reality is not visible. The repair starts with leaders, who have to show that bad news is welcome, for example by reporting their own missed commitments first.
blocks.title: Worked example: Kestrel Foods

blocks.text:
Generic answer: 'The Scrum values are commitment, courage, focus, openness and respect.' True for Scrum. The SAFe Core Values are alignment, transparency, respect for people and relentless improvement.

Outdated answer: 'alignment, built-in quality, transparency, program execution.' That is the earlier set.

Wrong fix: 'Roll the practices out more strictly.' SAFe answer: practices without the mindset give mechanical agility. Change the thinking, starting with leaders.
blocks.title: SAFe answer versus generic answer

blocks.text: For each Core Value, write one behaviour you have seen that supports it and one that undermines it. Then pick the value that is weakest where you work and write the first thing a leader, not a team, would have to do differently.
blocks.title: Guided activity (10 minutes)

lessons.title: 3 · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles and AI
lessons.summary: Each principle with its number, what it changes in practice, and how AI supports agility.

blocks.text: SAFe rests on ten Lean-Agile principles, which it calls immutable and underlying. Practices can be adapted to context; the principles are what the adaptation must honour. The exam refers to principles by number and by name, so learn both.
blocks.title: Why the principles matter

rows: Decisions weigh cost, value and Cost of Delay inside an economic framework
Optimise the whole value stream, not one department
Keep design options open until evidence allows a choice
Build incrementally with fast, integrated learning cycles
Integrate often so that feedback arrives early
Base milestones on objective evaluation of working systems
Judge progress by a working system, not by documents
Limit work in process, shrink batches, shorten queues
Apply cadence, synchronize with cross-domain planning
A shared rhythm and joint planning manage uncertainty
Unlock the intrinsic motivation of knowledge workers
Autonomy, mastery and purpose beat individual incentives
Decide locally what is frequent and time-critical
Structure people around value streams, not functions
blocks.title: The ten principles

blocks.text:
Principles 1 and 9 work together. Principle 9 says who decides; principle 1 gives them the economic framework to decide well. Without the framework, decentralised decisions are guesses.

Principles 3 and 5 are swapped most often. Link 3 with options, through set-based design, and 5 with milestones, through demonstrations of a working system.

Principles 4 and 7 both involve integration. Principle 4 is about learning from integrated increments. Principle 7 is about the rhythm that lets many teams plan and integrate at the same moment: cadence makes events predictable, and synchronisation brings perspectives together.

For principle 9, keep a decision central when it is infrequent, long-lasting and has significant economies of scale, such as a common technology platform. Decentralise everything else: decisions that are frequent, time-critical and need local information.
blocks.title: The pairs that are easy to confuse

blocks.text:
Brightwater's billing train has thirty features in progress and finishes two per PI. Every design change waits about a week for one architecture manager. The first integration of a new tariff engine is planned for month nine.

Reading it through the principles: thirty features in progress is a flow problem, principle 6, so the train limits work in process. The approval queue breaks principle 9, so the manager defines a decision framework and teams decide inside it. Integration in month nine ignores principle 4, so the engine is integrated every iteration and shown at the System Demo, which also satisfies principle 5.
blocks.title: Worked example: Brightwater Utilities

blocks.text:
SAFe's public guidance describes AI as a wide range of smart machines performing tasks that normally need human intelligence, and says it can be applied at all levels of SAFe: to build intelligent customer solutions, to automate value stream activities and to improve customer insight. It contrasts AI with conventional rule-based software for situations that predefined rules cannot cover.

The Leading SAFe course page lists three AI points for an Agilist: AI fundamentals and prompting for the role's duties, the SAFe CoPilot assistant, and human-in-the-loop evaluation of AI output. The practical rule is simple. Give the assistant the source material, the audience and the format you need, and have a person check the output before it informs a decision.
blocks.title: Empower agility with AI

blocks.text:
Manager decides: 'Ask the architecture manager to approve faster.' SAFe answer: decentralise the decision within a framework. A faster queue is still a queue.

Generic answer: 'Motivate developers with a bonus per story.' SAFe answer: principle 8, intrinsic motivation; individual targets harm teamwork.

Wrong principle: a department that optimises its own throughput and slows the train is a principle 2 problem, systems thinking, not a motivation problem.
blocks.title: SAFe answer versus generic answer

blocks.text: Cover the table and write the ten principles from memory, with numbers. Check, then repeat until the numbers are right. Next, describe one real delay from your own work in two sentences and name the principle it breaks and the first change that principle suggests.
blocks.title: Guided activity (15 minutes)

lessons.title: 4 · Team and technical agility
lessons.summary: Agile Teams, Agile Release Trains, built-in quality and the Continuous Delivery Pipeline.

blocks.text:
Team and Technical Agility has three dimensions: Agile Teams, Teams of Agile Teams, and Built-In Quality.

An Agile Team is a cross-functional group of typically ten or fewer people with all the skills needed to define, build, test and deliver value. It can be a technical team or a business team. Teams use SAFe Scrum, SAFe Team Kanban or a hybrid. Each team has two specific roles. The Product Owner maximises the value the team delivers by keeping the team backlog aligned with customer and stakeholder needs, and decides its order. The Scrum Master/Team Coach is a servant leader and coach who facilitates team events and helps the team improve; this person is usually not a people manager and does not assign tasks.
blocks.title: Agile Teams

blocks.text: An Agile Release Train, or ART, is a long-lived team of Agile teams that incrementally develops, delivers and often operates one or more solutions in a development value stream. It typically has 50 to 125 people. It is not a project: it is not formed for one release and disbanded afterwards.
blocks.title: The Agile Release Train

blocks.text: The System Team supports the train by building the development environment and helping with integration.
rows: Servant leader and coach for the train; facilitates ART events
Defines features, owns and prioritises the ART backlog
Defines the architecture, identifies nonfunctional requirements, designs interfaces
Key stakeholders responsible for governance, fitness for use and return on investment
blocks.title: Roles on the train

blocks.text: Built-In Quality is a set of practices that help the outputs of Agile teams meet quality standards throughout the creation of customer value. Quality is built in at every step; it is not inspected in by a test phase at the end. SAFe ties this to principle 6 and to shifting learning left, so problems are found when they are cheap to fix. The listed benefits include higher customer satisfaction, better velocity and delivery predictability, and better system performance. Cutting quality to go faster therefore makes a train slower.
blocks.title: Built-in quality

blocks.text: Deployment and release are separate: functionality can sit in production, hidden, until the business releases it.
rows: Explore the market and customer needs; define vision, roadmap and features
Make it available when the business chooses
Release in one event or in waves, by market need
blocks.title: The Continuous Delivery Pipeline

blocks.text: DevOps in SAFe is a mindset, a culture and a set of technical practices that support the integration, automation and collaboration needed to develop and operate a solution. It is not a team and not a toolset. SAFe's approach is CALMR: Culture, Automation, Lean flow, Measurement and Recovery. The general industry acronym is CALMS, ending in sharing; SAFe treats sharing as part of culture and adds recovery.
blocks.title: DevOps and CALMR

blocks.text:
Halden Freight's tracking train deploys a new route-pricing feature to production on Tuesday behind a feature switch. Customers see nothing. Product Management and the Business Owners decide to release it to ten large customers on the first of the month, when the new contracts start, and to everyone a month later.

Deployment was a technical event on Tuesday. Release was a business decision on a different date, in waves. The developers did not decide the release date, and neither did the RTE.
blocks.title: Worked example: Halden Freight

blocks.text:
Manager decides: 'The development manager sets the order of the team backlog.' SAFe answer: the Product Owner does.

Wrong role: 'The Scrum Master/Team Coach assigns tasks' or 'the RTE prioritises features.' SAFe answer: the coach facilitates and the team organises its own work; Product Management prioritises features.

Generic answer: 'Create a DevOps team' or 'add a testing phase at the end.' SAFe answer: DevOps is a shared mindset, and quality is built in throughout.
blocks.title: SAFe answer versus generic answer

blocks.text: Draw the four aspects of the pipeline as four boxes. Under each, write the activities from memory and one real example of the activity from a product you know. Mark where deployment ends and release begins, and write who would decide the release.

lessons.title: 5 · Customer centricity, design thinking and the ART backlog
lessons.summary: Building the right thing: customers, design thinking, features, enablers and WSJF.

blocks.text:
Customer Centricity is a mindset focused on creating positive customer experiences through the full set of products and services an enterprise offers. SAFe recognises internal customers, people inside the company who use what a train builds, and external customers, who buy or use the products. A platform train has customers too.

Design thinking is a customer-centric development process for creating desirable products that are profitable and sustainable over their life. Where a waterfall approach starts from requirements, design thinking starts from understanding the problem and the context of use. It alternates divergent thinking, which widens the set of possibilities, with convergent thinking, which narrows it to a choice. Its tools include personas, which are representative characterisations of users, and story maps.

Product Management is responsible for solutions that are desirable, viable, feasible and sustainable.
blocks.title: Customer centricity and design thinking

blocks.text:
The ART backlog holds the features and enablers that enhance the solution and extend its architectural runway, and it is managed as a Kanban system. A feature is solution functionality that delivers business value and is sized to be delivered by one ART within one PI. Product Management defines features and prioritises the backlog. The System Architect defines enablers. Teams split features into stories for their own team backlogs, which the Product Owners own.

Nonfunctional requirements, such as security and performance, are system qualities that constrain the design across the backlogs. Capacity allocation reserves a share of capacity for each type of work, so enablers and maintenance are not always outranked by features.
blocks.title: The ART backlog

blocks.text:
Weighted Shortest Job First sequences jobs to produce the best economic outcome. WSJF equals Cost of Delay divided by job duration, and job size is used as a proxy for duration.

Cost of Delay has three components: user-business value, time criticality, and risk reduction or opportunity enablement. All values are relative: jobs are compared with each other, usually with a modified Fibonacci scale, not priced in money. WSJF ignores sunk costs; only the remaining work counts. The job with the highest WSJF goes first.
blocks.title: Prioritising with WSJF

blocks.text: Refund status goes first. Loyalty tiers has the highest Cost of Delay but is so large that it scores lowest.
blocks.title: Worked example: a WSJF table at Verano Travel

blocks.text:
Wrong role: 'The RTE prioritises the ART backlog.' SAFe answer: Product Management does; the RTE facilitates.

Wrong level: 'A feature needs a Lean business case and an MVP.' Those belong to epics. A feature has a benefit hypothesis and acceptance criteria.

Generic answer: 'Finish what we have spent the most on' or 'do the most valuable first.' SAFe answer: WSJF ignores sunk cost and divides value by size, so a small, urgent job beats a large, valuable one.
blocks.title: SAFe answer versus generic answer

blocks.text: Take four pieces of work waiting in a backlog you know. Score each for value, time criticality and risk or opportunity using 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 and 20, starting each column by giving the smallest item a 1. Add the three for Cost of Delay, estimate size the same way, and divide. Compare the WSJF order with the order the work is really being done in, and note one reason for the difference.
blocks.title: Guided activity (15 minutes)

lessons.title: 6 · PI Planning and executing the PI
lessons.summary: The Planning Interval, the two-day planning event, the ART events and Inspect and Adapt.

blocks.text: A Planning Interval, or PI, is a cadence-based timebox in which a train delivers continuous value aligned with its PI objectives. It typically lasts 8 to 12 weeks, most often as four or five development iterations followed by one Innovation and Planning iteration. SAFe plans on this cadence but releases on demand: the PI is a planning rhythm, not a release schedule.
blocks.title: The Planning Interval

blocks.text:
PI Planning is a cadence-based event for the whole train that aligns teams and stakeholders to a shared mission and vision. It is typically a two-day event, facilitated by the Release Train Engineer, and everyone who does the work takes part.

Before the event the train prepares three kinds of readiness: organizational, content and logistics. The two primary outputs are committed PI objectives from each team and the ART planning board, which shows feature delivery dates and the dependencies between teams.

PI objectives summarise the business and technical goals a team intends to achieve. Each is committed or uncommitted. Uncommitted objectives cover planned work with significant uncertainty; they are left out of the commitment so that the commitment stays reliable.
blocks.title: PI Planning

blocks.text: This agenda is from author knowledge of SAFe 6; the public article shows only its introduction.
rows: Business context, product vision, architecture vision and planning context
Business Owner or executive, Product Management, System Architect, RTE
Team breakouts: draft plans, capacity, risks and dependencies
Draft plan review, then management review and problem-solving
RTE; managers adjust scope or resources
Planning adjustments, then team breakouts; Business Owners assign business value
Final plan review, ART risks, confidence vote, plan rework if needed, retrospective
blocks.title: How the two days usually run

blocks.text:
Risks that affect the train are discussed in front of everyone and placed in one of four categories, known as ROAM. Resolved: no longer a concern. Owned: someone takes responsibility for it after the event. Accepted: nothing more can be done, and the risk is understood. Mitigated: a plan exists to reduce its impact.

Each team, and then the whole train, holds a confidence vote, usually by showing one to five fingers. A low vote means the plan is not yet a commitment, and it is reworked. Business Owners assign business value from 1 to 10 to each team's objectives; that value is later compared with what was achieved.
blocks.title: Risks and the confidence vote

rows: Visibility into progress toward PI objectives, with scope adjustments
Combines the PO Sync and the Coach Sync
Integrated view of new features from all teams
Demonstrate, measure, and solve systemic problems
blocks.title: Events while the PI runs

blocks.text:
The Innovation and Planning iteration gives an estimating buffer for meeting PI objectives and dedicated time for innovation, continuing education, PI Planning and Inspect and Adapt. No feature work is planned into it. It is not a hardening or bug-fixing iteration.

Inspect and Adapt has three parts, in this order: the PI System Demo, a quantitative and qualitative measurement review, and a retrospective and problem-solving workshop. The workshop looks for root causes of systemic problems, and the improvement items it produces go into the ART backlog for the next PI Planning. The ART Predictability Measure compares the business value achieved with the business value planned.
blocks.title: The IP iteration and Inspect and Adapt

blocks.text: At Odell Health's PI Planning, the scheduling team depends on an interface a vendor may deliver late. The team writes that objective as uncommitted. At the end of day one the draft plans exceed capacity by a third, so the management review removes two features. On day two a risk about a data centre move cannot be settled; the infrastructure director takes it, so it is Owned. One team votes two fingers. The RTE does not close the event: the team explains its concern, a dependency is moved, and the second vote is four.
blocks.title: Worked example: Odell Health

blocks.text:
Generic answer: 'The sprint review shows progress.' SAFe answer: the Iteration Review covers one team; the System Demo shows the integrated work of the whole train each iteration.

Manager decides: 'Managers fix the plan after the event' or 'only team leads attend.' SAFe answer: the people who do the work make and own the plan, and the whole train attends.

Wrong role: 'Product Owners assign business value' or 'Product Management facilitates PI Planning.' SAFe answer: Business Owners assign business value, and the RTE facilitates.

Wrong use: 'Plan features into the IP iteration' or 'customers get releases once per PI.' SAFe answer: no feature work in the IP iteration, and release is on demand.
blocks.title: SAFe answer versus generic answer

blocks.text: Write four risks from a plan you know. Place each in a ROAM category and justify the choice in one sentence. For any you marked Owned, name the owner. Then write one objective from that plan as committed and one as uncommitted, and explain what uncertainty makes the second one uncommitted.

lessons.title: 7 · The SAFe portfolio and enterprise strategy
lessons.summary: What a portfolio is, the two kinds of value stream, Strategic Themes, the Portfolio Vision and the canvas.

blocks.text:
Lean Portfolio Management, or LPM, aligns strategy and execution by applying Lean and systems thinking to three areas: strategy and investment funding, Agile portfolio operations, and Lean governance.

A SAFe portfolio is a set of value streams that deliver solutions within common funding and governance. It is not a list of projects. The Enterprise is the business entity the portfolio belongs to; a small enterprise may have one portfolio and a large one several.
blocks.title: What Lean Portfolio Management is

blocks.text: Development value streams build the solutions that operational value streams use. Each development value stream has one or more ARTs.
rows: The activities that deliver a product or service to a customer
Taking a mortgage from application to payout
The activities that turn a business hypothesis into a digitally enabled solution
The trains that build the mortgage systems
blocks.title: Two kinds of value stream

blocks.text:
The enterprise strategy answers four questions: which customers and markets are served, which products and solutions are provided, what unique value and resources the enterprise brings, and how these will be extended in future.

Strategic Themes carry that strategy into the portfolio. They are portfolio-level business objectives that provide competitive differentiation and business context for decisions. SAFe recommends writing them as Objectives and Key Results, in plain business language. Portfolio leaders use them to steer, and trains refer to them when defining epics and features. An epic with no link to a theme should prompt a hard question.
blocks.title: Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy

blocks.text:
The Portfolio Vision describes the future state of the portfolio's value streams and solutions. It should be aspirational yet realistic, and motivating. It is a key input for identifying epics, and Business Owners or senior leaders typically present it at PI Planning.

The portfolio canvas, adapted from the Business Model Canvas, captures on one page the portfolio's development value streams, solutions, customers, revenue streams and other key elements. A canvas of the current state and a canvas of the future state show the gap, and epics are how the gap is closed. To generate options for the future state, SAFe uses a SWOT analysis followed by a TOWS analysis, which combines strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats into strategic options.
blocks.title: Vision and canvas

rows: Highest decision-making and financial accountability; approves epics
Coordinates an epic through the portfolio Kanban
Sets the portfolio's technology vision, strategy and roadmap
Supports LPM with governance and operations
Carry business responsibility on the trains
blocks.title: Roles at the portfolio level

blocks.text:
Quarry Insurance has one portfolio for personal lines. Its enterprise strategy is to grow among drivers under thirty. LPM writes a Strategic Theme as an objective, 'Become the easiest insurer for young drivers to join', with key results on quote completion rate and time to first policy.

An Epic Owner proposes rebuilding the agent commission system. It may be worthwhile, but it serves no theme, so Portfolio Leadership asks which objective it supports before spending analysis effort. A second epic, a five-minute mobile quote, maps directly to the theme and moves forward.
blocks.title: Worked example: Quarry Insurance

blocks.text:
Generic answer: 'A portfolio is the list of approved projects.' SAFe answer: a set of value streams under common funding and governance.

Wrong level: 'The System Architect sets the portfolio technology roadmap.' SAFe answer: the Enterprise Architect does; the System Architect works for one train.

Reversed pair: the operational value stream serves the customer, and the development value stream builds what it uses. Distractors swap them.

blocks.text: Name one operational value stream in an organisation you know and list its main steps from request to delivery. Underneath, list the systems each step depends on. lessons.title: 8 · Portfolio flow, epics, Lean budgets and guardrails
lessons.summary: How epics move through the portfolio Kanban, how value streams are funded and how spending is governed.

blocks.text:
An epic is a significant solution development initiative. SAFe is explicit that an epic is not a project. Business epics deliver value directly to customers; enabler epics extend the architectural runway for future business or technical needs.

Because of its size, every epic needs a Lean business case and a minimum viable product, and it must be approved by Portfolio Leadership. An Epic Owner coordinates it through the portfolio Kanban. The MVP is an early, minimal version of the solution whose job is to prove or disprove the epic's hypothesis. After the MVP comes the decision SAFe takes from the Lean Startup cycle: pivot, persevere or stop. Approval of an epic is approval to test a hypothesis, not a promise to build the full scope.
blocks.title: Epics

blocks.text: The state names are from author knowledge of SAFe 6; the public article confirms the Kanban but not its states.
rows: All large ideas are captured; no analysis yet
The idea is shaped into an epic hypothesis statement and roughly sized
Lean business case and MVP are defined; go or no-go decision
Approved epics wait until a train has capacity to pull them
The MVP is built and evaluated; then persevere, pivot or stop
The epic is finished because the hypothesis was proven or abandoned
blocks.title: The portfolio Kanban

blocks.text:
Lean Budgets are a financial governance approach that funds value streams instead of projects. Traditional project funding creates overhead: each project needs its own approval, people are moved to the work, and any change triggers re-approval. With a funded value stream, stable teams stay in place and the work comes to them. When a feature takes longer than expected, priorities are adjusted locally inside the budget; no change request is needed.

Each portfolio operates within a budget that comes from the enterprise's strategic planning, and LPM allocates it to value streams. Stakeholders decide the allocation together in a participatory budgeting event, which the current glossary also calls Strategic Investment Planning.
blocks.title: Lean budgets

blocks.text: Investment horizons run from Horizon 0, solutions being retired, to Horizon 3, early evaluation of new opportunities.
rows: The balance of spending between today's solutions and future ones
Applying capacity allocation to optimize value and solution integrity
The mix of features, enablers and maintenance
Portfolio review of epics above a threshold
Ongoing business involvement in priorities and results
blocks.title: The four Lean budget guardrails

blocks.text: The cadence of participatory budgeting is from author knowledge.
rows: Quarterly, at least a month before the next PI Planning
Strategy, budget and progress toward the vision
Allocating the portfolio budget to value streams
blocks.title: Portfolio events

blocks.text:
Larkspur's depot-automation value stream has a budget for the year. An Epic Owner proposes self-service returns kiosks. In Analyzing, the Lean business case states the hypothesis, 'kiosks cut returns handling time by half', and an MVP of three kiosks in one depot. Portfolio Leadership approves it, although the value stream is already funded, because the initiative is above the portfolio's epic threshold.

The MVP shows a 15 percent saving, not 50. The sponsor argues for the full rollout because the epic was approved. LPM instead pivots to kiosks for business customers only, where the saving was largest. Nothing was re-approved by finance: the value stream budget did not change.
blocks.title: Worked example: Larkspur Logistics

blocks.text:
Generic answer: 'An epic is a project' or 'it is done when its scope is delivered.' SAFe answer: an epic tests a hypothesis with an MVP and ends in pivot, persevere or stop.

Wrong role: 'The Epic Owner approves the epic.' SAFe answer: Portfolio Leadership approves; the Epic Owner coordinates.

Manager decides: 'Raise a change request for more funding.' SAFe answer: the value stream budget stays, and priorities are adjusted locally.

Wrong fate for the PMO: SAFe does not abolish it; it commonly evolves into a Value Management Office.
blocks.title: SAFe answer versus generic answer

blocks.text: Choose a large initiative you know. Write its hypothesis in one sentence that could be proven false. Define the smallest MVP that would test it and the measure you would look at. Then write what result would make you pivot and what result would make you stop.

lessons.title: 9 · Lead the change
lessons.summary: Leading by example, the implementation roadmap, the tipping point and how leaders use AI.

blocks.text:
Lean-Agile Leadership describes how leaders drive and sustain organisational change and operational excellence by empowering individuals and teams to reach their highest potential. They do this by leading by example, by learning and modelling the Lean-Agile mindset, values, principles and practices, and by leading the change to the new way of working.

The core argument is that only managers, executives and other leaders can change the systems that govern how work is done: budgeting, incentives, approval boards, organisational structure. Teams cannot change those. A transformation that is delegated therefore stalls at exactly the points where it matters.
blocks.title: Lean-Agile leadership

blocks.text:
The SAFe Implementation Roadmap starts with reaching the tipping point: the moment when the overriding organisational imperative is to achieve the change, not to resist it. SAFe names two ways to get there. A burning platform is an obvious failure to compete. Proactive leadership is leaders who see the need before a crisis and set out a compelling vision.

A vision for change provides three things: purpose, motivation and alignment. A vision alone is not enough. Following John Kotter, whose work the roadmap draws on, SAFe calls for a sufficiently powerful guiding coalition: influential, respected people who can secure resources and overcome resistance. SAFe Practice Consultants act as change agents, and a Lean-Agile Center of Excellence, a small Agile team dedicated to implementing the new way of working, usually supports the effort. SAFe recommends that senior leaders attend Leading SAFe themselves.
blocks.title: Reaching the tipping point

blocks.text: SAFe notes that in practice the steps are not perfectly sequential.
rows: Create a Lean-Agile Center of Excellence
Launch More ARTs and Value Streams
blocks.title: The SAFe Implementation Roadmap

blocks.text: The Leading SAFe course adds AI to the leader's toolkit: fundamentals and prompting for the role, the SAFe CoPilot assistant, and human-in-the-loop evaluation of output. For a leader the principle is that AI prepares and people decide. An assistant can summarise Inspect and Adapt findings, compare options or draft a communication. The leader evaluates what it produced, checks it against reality and stays accountable for the decision. AI output does not replace the objective evidence of a working system, and confidential data goes only into approved tools.
blocks.title: Empower leaders with AI

blocks.text:
Pinecrest's teams run iterations well, yet the annual budget cycle, individual performance rankings and a weekly change approval board are untouched. The head of delivery has asked an Agile coach to 'finish the transformation'.

The coach cannot change any of those three systems. The SAFe reading is that the tipping point was never reached at leadership level and there is no guiding coalition. The next steps are for executives to attend Leading SAFe, form the coalition with a Lean-Agile Center of Excellence, and take ownership of the budgeting and approval changes themselves.
blocks.title: Worked example: Pinecrest Telecom

blocks.text:
Wrong owner: 'The coaches, the PMO or the RTE lead the transformation.' SAFe answer: leaders do, since only they can change the system.

Generic answer: 'Start by training the teams and launching a train.' SAFe answer: the roadmap starts with the tipping point, change agents and leaders; teams are trained at launch.

Manager abdicates: 'The AI recommended it, so we did it.' SAFe answer: a person evaluates the output and remains accountable.
blocks.title: SAFe answer versus generic answer

blocks.text: List three policies in an organisation you know that teams cannot change and that slow delivery. For each, name the leader who could change it. Then write the two-sentence vision you would give that group of leaders: why change, and what will be different in a year.
