questions.prompt: How does SAFe define Business Agility?

options.text: Giving every team the freedom to choose its own goals, tools and release dates
Reducing the cost of IT delivery by moving development work to the lowest-cost locations
Running all projects in two-week sprints so that scope can be changed at any moment by the sponsor
Competing and thriving in the digital age by responding quickly with digitally enabled solutions

questions.explanation: SAFe defines Business Agility as the ability to compete and thrive in the digital age by responding quickly to market changes and opportunities with digitally enabled business solutions. Sprints alone are the generic Agile answer: they describe a team practice, not an enterprise capability.

questions.prompt: Marrow Retail has grown a deep hierarchy, and new digital products now take years to launch. Which response matches SAFe's dual operating system?

options.text: Add project managers to speed up each handoff
Dissolve the hierarchy and let teams self-assign
Create a new innovation department under the CIO
Add a value stream network beside the hierarchy

questions.explanation: SAFe follows Kotter: keep the hierarchy for stability and efficiency, and add a network organised around value streams for speed and adaptability. Dissolving the hierarchy is the tempting radical answer, but SAFe keeps both operating systems.

questions.prompt: In SAFe's dual operating system, what is each side optimised for?

options.text: The network for long-term strategy, the hierarchy for daily delivery
The network for governance and compliance, the hierarchy for innovation and learning
The network for speed and adaptability, the hierarchy for efficiency and stability
The network for cost reduction, the hierarchy for customer experience

questions.explanation: The value stream network gives speed and adaptability while the hierarchy keeps efficiency and stability. The first distractor reverses the roles: compliance and governance functions live in the hierarchy.

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of SAFe's seven core competencies?

options.text: Lean Portfolio Management
Project Portfolio Control
Scrum of Scrums Governance
Agile Maturity Auditing

questions.explanation: Lean Portfolio Management is one of the seven core competencies of Business Agility. Project portfolio control sounds close, but SAFe replaces project-based control with Lean portfolio practices.

questions.prompt: A portfolio funds a minimum viable product, and the evidence shows that customers do not want it. In the Business Agility Value Stream, what comes next?

options.text: A full business case for the next phase
A pivot-or-persevere decision
Delivery of the remaining planned scope
A handover to operations

questions.explanation: After the MVP is delivered, the value stream reaches Pivot or Persevere, where evidence decides what happens to the investment. Continuing with the planned scope is the traditional project answer, which ignores what the MVP has just taught.

questions.prompt: Arrange these steps of the Business Agility Value Stream in order.

options.text: Connect to Customer
Pivot or Persevere
Organize Around Value
Sense Opportunity
Deliver MVP
Fund MVP

questions.explanation: The value stream starts by sensing an opportunity and funding an MVP, then organises around value, connects to the customer, delivers the MVP and decides to pivot or persevere. Funding comes before organising: the MVP is funded first and people are then organised around it.

questions.prompt: Which three measurement domains does SAFe use to assess progress toward Business Agility?

options.text: Velocity, utilisation and defects
Strategy, structure and culture
Scope, schedule and budget
Flow, outcomes and competency

questions.explanation: SAFe measures flow, outcomes and competency. Scope, schedule and budget is the traditional project triangle, which measures conformance to a plan, not agility.

questions.prompt: Tessel Bank's leaders say that every business is now a software business. What does this mean for the bank?

options.text: Its competitiveness depends on digitally enabled solutions
Its products should all be rebuilt as cloud services
Its branches should be closed in favour of a mobile app
Its IT department should report directly to marketing

questions.explanation: SAFe places enterprises in the age of software and digital, where the ability to deliver digitally enabled solutions decides who thrives. The statement is about capability, not about a particular channel or architecture choice.

questions.prompt: According to the view SAFe borrows from Kotter, what happens as a successful startup grows?

options.text: Its hierarchy disappears once the teams have become self-managing
Its growing hierarchy starts to crowd out the entrepreneurial network
Its hierarchy and its network merge into one matrix organisation
Its entrepreneurial network naturally takes over from the hierarchy

questions.explanation: Organisations start as a network, add hierarchy to scale, and over time the hierarchy's demands overtake the network. A matrix is a common real-world response, but it is not the dual operating system SAFe describes.

questions.prompt: An enterprise wants the simplest starting point for implementing SAFe with one Agile Release Train. Which configuration fits?

options.text: Portfolio SAFe
Essential SAFe
Large Solution SAFe
Full SAFe

questions.explanation: Essential SAFe holds the minimal elements an ART needs and is the simplest place to start. Full SAFe is the most comprehensive configuration, for portfolios of large and complex solutions.

questions.prompt: Executives at Halden Freight want Business Agility and ask the PMO to run the transformation while they focus on operations. What is SAFe's view?

options.text: Leaders must lead the change themselves
Agile coaches should own the transformation
The PMO is the right owner of the change
Each team should transform at its own pace

questions.explanation: SAFe holds that only leaders can change the system, so they must lead by example and lead the change. Handing the transformation to coaches is the tempting answer, but coaches support the change; they cannot alter the system that governs how work is done.

questions.prompt: A portfolio wants to know whether its solutions are achieving the intended business benefits. Which measurement domain answers this?

options.text: Predictability
Outcomes
Flow
Competency

questions.explanation: Outcomes, measured with value stream KPIs, show whether solutions deliver business benefit. Flow shows how efficiently value moves through the system, which says nothing about whether it was worth delivering.

questions.prompt: What does the Lean-Agile Mindset combine?

options.text: Lean thinking and the Agile Manifesto
Six Sigma and the PMBOK Guide
DevOps tooling and design sprint workshops
Agile ceremonies and Kanban boards

questions.explanation: SAFe describes the mindset as the beliefs and actions of people who embrace Lean thinking and the Agile Manifesto. Scrum and Kanban are practices that express the mindset; they are not the mindset.

questions.prompt: Which set lists the four SAFe Core Values?

options.text: Commitment, courage, focus, openness, and respect for other team members
Autonomy, mastery, purpose, psychological safety at work
Alignment, transparency, respect for people, relentless improvement
Alignment, built-in quality, transparency, program execution

questions.explanation: The current core values are alignment, transparency, respect for people and relentless improvement. The set with built-in quality and program execution is the earlier version of the values, which makes it the trap.

questions.prompt: Match each SAFe Core Value to a leader behaviour that expresses it.

options.text: Growing people and valuing different viewpoints
Reflecting at milestones and acting on what is learned
Making progress and problems visible without blame
Connecting strategy to backlogs through a shared vision
Rewarding the individual who works the longest hours

questions.explanation: Alignment connects strategy to execution, transparency makes reality visible, respect for people develops and values them, and relentless improvement turns reflection into action. Alignment and transparency are the pair most often confused: one is about direction, the other about visibility.

questions.prompt: Teams at Kestrel Foods report every feature as on track until the week of the release, so leaders learn of delays when it is too late to act. Which Core Value is most directly missing?

options.text: Transparency
Alignment
Relentless improvement
Respect for people

questions.explanation: Transparency means that facts, including bad news, are visible in time to act on them. Alignment is the tempting alternative, but the teams may agree fully on the goal; what is absent is visibility of the real status.

questions.prompt: Six teams on a train each deliver what their own manager asks for, and the combined result serves no clear customer goal. Which Core Value is most directly missing?

options.text: Transparency
Alignment
Relentless improvement
Respect for people

questions.explanation: Alignment keeps everyone working toward the same vision and objectives. The teams may be perfectly transparent about their work and still pull in different directions.

questions.prompt: Which of these belongs to Lean thinking as SAFe summarises it?

options.text: Maximise the utilisation of experts
Let the customer pull value
Batch releases to cut overhead
Push work to keep everyone busy

questions.explanation: Lean thinking specifies value, identifies the value stream, makes value flow, lets the customer pull value and pursues perfection. Maximising utilisation is the classic opposite: it creates queues and slows flow.

questions.prompt: A company has adopted stand-ups, boards and two-week iterations, yet decisions, funding and deadlines work as they did before. What does SAFe say is missing?

options.text: A change of mindset, since agility is more than practices
A stricter rollout of the practices across all the teams
A dedicated tool to track compliance with the ceremonies
A longer iteration length that gives teams more time

questions.explanation: SAFe stresses that agility is a mindset change, not only a set of practices. Rolling the practices out more strictly is the tempting answer, and it produces the same mechanical result on a larger scale.

questions.prompt: Which statement is one of the four values of the Agile Manifesto?

options.text: Processes and tools over individuals and interactions
Comprehensive documentation over working software
Responding to change over following a plan
Contract negotiation over customer collaboration

questions.explanation: The manifesto values responding to change over following a plan. The other three options reverse the manifesto's own pairs, placing the item it values less in front.

questions.prompt: Match each SAFe Lean-Agile Principle number to its name.

options.text: Maximize the utilization of specialists
Take an economic view
Decentralize decision-making
Make value flow without interruptions
Build incrementally with fast, integrated learning cycles

questions.explanation: The ten principles are numbered, and the exam uses the numbers. Principle #1 is the economic view, #4 is incremental building with learning cycles, #6 is flow and #9 is decentralised decisions; the extra option is not a SAFe principle at all.

questions.prompt: Match each of these SAFe Lean-Agile Principle numbers to its name.

options.text: Deliver working software at the end of each sprint
Apply systems thinking
Assume variability; preserve options
Base milestones on objective evaluation of working systems
Apply cadence, synchronize with cross-domain planning

questions.explanation: Principle #2 is systems thinking, #3 is variability and options, #5 is objective milestones and #7 is cadence and synchronisation. Numbers 3 and 5 are swapped most often, so link #3 with options and #5 with milestones.

questions.prompt: Which is SAFe Lean-Agile Principle #10?

options.text: Organize around value
Unlock the intrinsic motivation of knowledge workers
Take an economic view
Apply systems thinking

questions.explanation: Principle #10 is Organize around value, the last of the ten. Unlocking intrinsic motivation is Principle #8 and is the usual wrong pick, because both sit near the end of the list.

questions.prompt: A product manager must choose between delaying a feature by one PI and paying for extra capacity now. Which principle asks for this decision to be framed in terms of Cost of Delay?

options.text: #9 Decentralize decision-making
#7 Apply cadence, synchronize with cross-domain planning
#1 Take an economic view
#3 Assume variability; preserve options

questions.explanation: Principle #1 asks for decisions to be made in a proper economic context, which includes the Cost of Delay. Principle #9 covers who decides; Principle #1 covers the economic reasoning used to decide.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe ask leaders to give teams an economic framework such as guardrails and Cost of Delay?

options.text: So that every decision is escalated for approval
So that teams can be ranked by cost efficiency
So that budgets can be fixed for several years
So that local decisions rest on sound trade-offs

questions.explanation: An economic framework lets people decide locally and still decide well, connecting Principle #1 to Principle #9. Escalating every decision is the opposite of the intent: the framework exists so that approval queues are not needed.

questions.prompt: A test department maximises its own throughput by testing in large batches, and the end-to-end delivery time of the train gets worse. Which principle explains what went wrong?

options.text: #8 Unlock the intrinsic motivation of knowledge workers
#5 Base milestones on objective evaluation of working systems
#2 Apply systems thinking
#10 Organize around value

questions.explanation: Systems thinking says that optimising a component does not optimise the system. The test department improved its local measure and harmed the whole value stream, which is the pattern Principle #2 warns about.

questions.prompt: Architects at Brightwater Utilities must choose a messaging technology, and the best choice depends on load data that will exist only after two more iterations. What does Principle #3 advise?

options.text: Pick the most familiar option now to avoid any delay
Ask the steering committee to choose on the team's behalf
Keep several design options open until the data arrives
Freeze the requirements so that the choice is simpler

questions.explanation: Principle #3 preserves options through set-based design, keeping alternatives alive until learning allows a sound choice. Choosing early is the point-based approach, which the principle says is often wrong.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe consider an early commitment to a single design risky?

options.text: Designs that are chosen early cost more to build than later ones
Architects lose motivation when the design is fixed before they start
Uncertainty is highest at the start, so the early choice is often wrong
Early commitment prevents the team from using cadence and synchronisation

questions.explanation: Early in development the cone of uncertainty is at its widest, so a single point-based choice made then is frequently wrong and expensive to reverse. Variability is not bad in itself; committing before learning is.

questions.prompt: A solution is designed for nine months before any part of it is assembled, so the teams get no feedback on their design assumptions until the end. Which principle does this most directly ignore?

options.text: #8 Unlock the intrinsic motivation of knowledge workers
#4 Build incrementally with fast, integrated learning cycles
#5 Base milestones on objective evaluation of working systems
#7 Apply cadence, synchronize with cross-domain planning

questions.explanation: Principle #4 calls for building in increments so that integrated results give fast feedback. Nine months without integration postpones all learning to the end, when changing course costs the most.

questions.prompt: A steering committee approves each phase when its documents are signed off. What would Principle #5 use as a milestone?

options.text: A signed requirements specification for the phase
A demonstration of the integrated, working system
A percentage of the budget spent to date
A status report with a green traffic light

questions.explanation: Principle #5 bases milestones on objective evaluation of working systems, using integration points to show real progress. Signed documents are the phase-gate answer and show only that documents exist.

questions.prompt: Why are phase-gate milestones a weak indicator of progress in SAFe's view?

options.text: Documents can be complete while the solution still does not work
Gates measure the working system when they should measure plans
Phase gates take place too often to be of use to stakeholders
Stakeholders are unable to attend reviews at the end of a phase

questions.explanation: Phase gates assess plans and documents, so they can all pass while integration risk stays hidden. Only an evaluation of working, integrated increments gives objective evidence.

questions.prompt: A train has thirty features in progress and finishes two per PI. Which principle addresses this most directly?

options.text: #8 Unlock the intrinsic motivation of knowledge workers
#6 Make value flow without interruptions
#3 Assume variability; preserve options
#5 Base milestones on objective evaluation of working systems

questions.explanation: Too much work in process blocks flow, and Principle #6 is about making value move smoothly and quickly through the value stream. The situation is a flow problem, not a motivation or milestone problem.

questions.prompt: Which action improves flow?

options.text: Releasing less frequently
Starting more work in parallel
Reducing the size of work batches
Keeping each specialist fully utilised

questions.explanation: Smaller batches move through the system faster and give earlier feedback. Starting more work in parallel feels productive, but it raises work in process and lengthens every queue.

questions.prompt: Teams on a train use different iteration lengths and start dates, so the train has no common rhythm and its events never line up. Which principle addresses this?

options.text: #9 Decentralize decision-making
#4 Build incrementally with fast, integrated learning cycles
#7 Apply cadence, synchronize with cross-domain planning
#2 Apply systems thinking

questions.explanation: Principle #7 uses a shared cadence and synchronisation so that teams plan and integrate together. Systems thinking is the tempting alternative, but the specific gap here is the missing common rhythm.

questions.prompt: What do cadence and synchronisation each contribute?

options.text: Cadence removes variability from the work; synchronisation removes dependencies between teams
Cadence integrates the work of the teams; synchronisation sets the release dates in advance
Cadence fixes the scope of each increment; synchronisation fixes the size of each team
Cadence makes events predictable; synchronisation lets perspectives be integrated together

questions.explanation: Cadence gives a predictable rhythm, and synchronisation causes several perspectives to be understood, resolved and integrated at one time. Neither removes variability; together they help manage it.

questions.prompt: A manager proposes an individual bonus for the developer who closes the most stories. What is SAFe's view under Principle #8?

options.text: Knowledge workers are moved more by autonomy, mastery and purpose
Story counts are a sound basis for comparing people fairly
Bonuses should be paid to the Product Owner, not to developers
Individual bonuses are the strongest motivator for complex work

questions.explanation: Principle #8 says that knowledge work is driven by intrinsic motivation and that extrinsic rewards can degrade performance on problem-solving tasks. Individual targets also set team members against each other.

questions.prompt: Which idea, credited to Peter Drucker, supports Principle #8?

options.text: Knowledge workers need closer supervision than manual workers do
Knowledge workers produce more when their tasks are standardised
Knowledge workers know more about their work than their managers do
Knowledge workers respond best to pay that depends on output

questions.explanation: Drucker's point is that knowledge workers understand their own work better than anyone above them. The leader's job therefore shifts from directing tasks to creating an environment in which people can do their best work.

questions.prompt: Which decision is the best candidate to keep centralised under Principle #9?

options.text: Deciding when a team holds its retrospective
Choosing a common technology platform for the whole portfolio
Deciding how a team should split one of its larger user stories
Choosing the order of work within a team's iteration

questions.explanation: Strategic decisions that are global, long-lasting and bring economies of scale are worth centralising. The other decisions are frequent, local and time-critical, and belong with the people who have the context.

questions.prompt: Which decision should be decentralised under Principle #9?

options.text: How much budget each value stream receives
How a team sequences the stories in its own backlog
Which enterprise-wide cloud provider to standardise on
Which strategic themes the portfolio will pursue

questions.explanation: Frequent, time-critical decisions that need local information belong with the team. Strategic themes and budgets are infrequent, long-lasting and global, so they are decided centrally.

questions.prompt: Every design change waits a week in the queue of one architecture manager, and delivery has slowed. What is the SAFe answer?

options.text: Ask the manager to work through the queue more quickly
Define a decision framework and let teams decide within it
Move all design decisions to the PI Planning event
Add a second manager so that approvals are shared

questions.explanation: Principle #9 removes the approval queue by decentralising decisions inside a clear framework. A faster manager is the trap: the manager is still deciding where the team should, and the queue comes back.

questions.prompt: Analysts, developers and testers sit in separate departments, and each feature crosses five handoffs. Which principle addresses the cause?

options.text: #5 Base milestones on objective evaluation of working systems
#1 Take an economic view
#10 Organize around value
#7 Apply cadence, synchronize with cross-domain planning

questions.explanation: Principle #10 organises people around the flow of value, in value streams and trains, to remove handoffs between functional silos. Cadence would line up the departments' calendars and leave the handoffs in place.

questions.prompt: A recommended SAFe practice does not fit a team's regulatory context. What should guide the adaptation?

options.text: The practice as written, without change
The process used before SAFe
The preference of the most senior manager
The underlying Lean-Agile principles

questions.explanation: SAFe describes its principles as immutable and underlying, so practices can be adapted as long as the principles are honoured. Following the practice unchanged puts the mechanics above their purpose.

questions.prompt: According to SAFe's public guidance, where can AI be applied?

options.text: At all levels of SAFe, in solutions, value streams and customer insight
At the portfolio level, as a tool for automating funding decisions
At the team level, as a tool for writing and testing code more quickly
In a separate data science department that serves the trains

questions.explanation: The guidance says AI can be applied at all SAFe levels: to build intelligent customer solutions, automate value stream activities and improve customer insight. Treating AI as a coding tool for teams is the narrow view the guidance moves beyond.

questions.prompt: An Agilist asks an AI assistant to summarise the risks raised in PI Planning for a leadership update. What should happen before the summary is sent?

options.text: The summary is shortened so that any errors matter less
The summary is sent quickly, since speed is the benefit of AI
The assistant is asked to confirm that the summary is right
A person evaluates the output against what was actually said

questions.explanation: The course stresses human-in-the-loop evaluation of AI output, so a person checks the summary before it informs decisions. Asking the assistant to confirm its own work adds no independent check.

questions.prompt: Which prompt is most likely to give an Agilist a useful draft for a stakeholder update?

options.text: Make the perfect update that every stakeholder will love and that leaves no question open
Summarise all the important points
Summarise these PI objectives for business owners in five bullets, with risks first
Write something good about our PI

questions.explanation: A useful prompt gives the source material, the audience, the format and the emphasis. The long prompt that asks for perfection is the trap, since it adds words without adding any direction.

questions.prompt: According to SAFe's guidance, which kind of problem suits AI better than conventional rule-based software?

options.text: Situations that predefined rules cannot cover
Processes with a small number of fixed steps
Reports that follow a standard template
Calculations that must give exact results

questions.explanation: The guidance contrasts rule-based software with AI for scenarios that predefined rules cannot cover. Fixed steps and exact calculations are where conventional software remains the better tool.

questions.prompt: How does SAFe describe an Agile Team?

options.text: A group of specialists in one discipline who hand finished work to the next department
A temporary group formed for one project and disbanded when the project closes
A cross-functional group of ten or fewer who can define, build, test and deliver value
A group of any size that reports to a single project manager

questions.explanation: An Agile Team is cross-functional, typically ten or fewer people, with all the skills to define, build, test and deliver. A single-discipline team is the functional silo that cross-functional teams replace.

questions.prompt: Which two roles does every SAFe Agile Team include?

options.text: Product Owner and Scrum Master/Team Coach
Project Manager and Business Analyst
Product Manager and Business Owner
Release Train Engineer and System Architect

questions.explanation: Each Agile Team has a Product Owner and a Scrum Master/Team Coach. The Release Train Engineer and System Architect are real SAFe roles, which makes them tempting, but they serve the whole train.

questions.prompt: A new team expects its Scrum Master/Team Coach to hand out tasks and chase individuals for status. What is the role in SAFe?

options.text: A technical lead who makes the design decisions for the team
A servant leader who coaches the team and facilitates its events
A project manager who owns the schedule and reports on scope
A line manager who allocates the work and appraises each member

questions.explanation: The Scrum Master/Team Coach is a servant leader and coach and is usually not a people manager. Assigning tasks is the traditional management answer; in SAFe the team organises its own work.

questions.prompt: On a SAFe Agile Team, who decides the order of the work in the team backlog?

options.text: The Product Owner
The Scrum Master/Team Coach
The Release Train Engineer
The development manager

questions.explanation: The Product Owner maximises the value the team delivers by keeping the team backlog aligned with customer and stakeholder needs. A manager deciding the order is the trap: priority belongs to the Product Owner, not to the reporting line.

questions.prompt: How many people does an Agile Release Train typically include?

options.text: 5 to 11

questions.explanation: An ART is typically 50 to 125 people. Five to eleven is the size of a single team, not of a team of teams.

questions.prompt: Match each Agile Release Train role to its main responsibility.

options.text: Responsible for governance, fitness for use and return on investment
Assigns daily tasks to individual team members
Defines the architecture and identifies nonfunctional requirements
Servant leader and coach for the train
Defines features and prioritises the ART backlog

questions.explanation: The RTE coaches the train, Product Management owns what gets built, the System Architect guides the technical design and Business Owners carry business responsibility. Nobody on the train assigns daily tasks to individuals; teams manage their own work.

questions.prompt: A company forms a group of teams to deliver one release and plans to disband it afterwards. How does this differ from an Agile Release Train?

options.text: An ART is long-lived and keeps delivering in a value stream
An ART delivers one release and is then re-formed
An ART has no teams, only individual specialists
An ART is disbanded sooner, at the end of each Planning Interval

questions.explanation: An ART is a long-lived team of Agile teams that incrementally develops, delivers and often operates solutions in a development value stream. Forming and disbanding around a release is project thinking.

questions.prompt: Which three dimensions make up Team and Technical Agility?

options.text: People and skills, process and flow, technology and tools
Scrum teams, Kanban teams, Extreme Programming teams
Agile Teams, Teams of Agile Teams, Built-In Quality
Planning, execution and delivery, retrospection

questions.explanation: The competency has three dimensions: Agile Teams, Teams of Agile Teams and Built-In Quality. Scrum and Kanban are methods teams use inside the first dimension; they are not the dimensions.

questions.prompt: One team provides self-service build and hosting services so that other teams on the train can deliver without waiting. Which team topology is this?

options.text: Enabling team
Complicated subsystem team
Platform team
Stream-aligned team

questions.explanation: A platform team provides services that reduce the load on stream-aligned teams. A stream-aligned team is the one that delivers value directly along a flow of work to a customer.

questions.prompt: A train builds for five iterations and plans a testing phase at the end of the PI. What is SAFe's view?

options.text: The testing phase should be moved into the following PI
A testing phase is acceptable when a separate team carries it out
Quality has to be built in throughout, not inspected in at the end
End-of-PI testing is preferred, since it is more efficient

questions.explanation: Built-In Quality means quality practices run throughout development and shift learning to the left. A late test phase finds problems when they are most expensive to fix.

questions.prompt: A train drops automated tests to finish more stories this PI. What does SAFe predict?

options.text: Velocity and predictability fall as rework accumulates
Velocity rises for good, since testing was waste
Quality is unaffected, since demos reveal defects
Predictability improves, since the scope is smaller

questions.explanation: SAFe lists improved velocity and delivery predictability among the benefits of Built-In Quality, so removing it erodes both. The belief that tests are waste is the trap: the time saved returns later as rework.

questions.prompt: Arrange the four aspects of the Continuous Delivery Pipeline in order.

options.text: Continuous Deployment
Continuous Integration
Continuous Exploration
Release on Demand

questions.explanation: The pipeline runs from Continuous Exploration through Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment to Release on Demand. Deployment comes before release: solutions reach production first and are released when the business chooses.

questions.prompt: Arrange the four activities of Continuous Integration in order.

options.text: Build
Develop
Test end-to-end
Stage

questions.explanation: Continuous Integration develops, builds, tests end-to-end and stages the solution. Staging comes last: the solution is validated in a staging environment before it moves on to deployment.

questions.prompt: A feature is running in production behind a switch, invisible to customers, until marketing is ready. Which SAFe concept is this?

options.text: Separating deployment from release
Set-based design of the architecture
Continuous Exploration of customer needs
Synchronisation of the release train

questions.explanation: SAFe decouples deployment from release, so changes can reach production without changing what customers see. Release then becomes a business decision that needs no new deployment.

questions.prompt: What does CALMR stand for in SAFe's approach to DevOps?

options.text: Cadence, Alignment, Learning, Metrics, Release
Collaboration, Agility, Leadership, Monitoring, Reliability
Culture, Automation, Lean flow, Measurement, Recovery
Culture, Automation, Lean flow, Measurement, Sharing

questions.explanation: CALMR is culture, automation, lean flow, measurement and recovery. The version ending in sharing is CALMS, the general DevOps acronym; SAFe replaces sharing with recovery and treats sharing as part of culture.

questions.prompt: In SAFe, who decides when deployed functionality is released to customers?

options.text: The Release Train Engineer, at the end of every PI
The business, through Product Management and Business Owners
The operations team, when production capacity allows
The developers, as soon as the code has passed all of its automated tests

questions.explanation: Release on Demand makes release a business decision based on market and customer needs, answered by Product Management and Business Owners. Releasing at each PI boundary confuses the planning cadence with release.

questions.prompt: A company responds to slow releases by creating a DevOps team that sits between development and operations. What is SAFe's view?

options.text: DevOps is a mindset, a culture and practices shared by all, not another silo
A separate DevOps team is the recommended first step for any newly launched train
DevOps applies to operations staff and not to the Agile teams
DevOps is a set of tools, so a dedicated tooling team is sufficient

questions.explanation: SAFe defines DevOps as a mindset, a culture and a set of technical practices that break down the silos between those who build and those who operate. A team placed between the two adds a third silo.

questions.prompt: How does SAFe define Customer Centricity?

options.text: A rule that customers approve each requirement before work begins
A mindset focused on positive customer experiences across products and services
A department that collects customer complaints and reports the trends to management
A metric that tracks the number of features delivered per customer

questions.explanation: Customer Centricity is a mindset focused on creating positive customer experiences through the full set of products and services. It is not a department or a sign-off step, which is how traditional organisations often treat the customer.

questions.prompt: A platform train builds services that are used only by other trains inside the company. Who are its customers in SAFe's terms?

options.text: The external buyers of the company's end products alone
Internal customers, the groups that use its services
The executives who approved the platform's budget
It has no customers, since nobody pays for the services

questions.explanation: SAFe distinguishes internal customers, who use what a train builds inside the company, from external ones. A platform still has customers, and treating it as having none is how platforms drift from real needs.

questions.prompt: A sponsor wants a full requirements specification signed off before any customer has been consulted. How does design thinking differ?

options.text: It replaces customer research with rapid coding
It fixes the solution first and then looks for users who might want it
It postpones all design until after the release
It starts by understanding the problem and the context of use

questions.explanation: Design thinking focuses on understanding the problem, the context of use and how the solution evolves, where a waterfall approach focuses on requirements. It does not skip research; it starts with it.

questions.prompt: Which four qualities should a solution defined by Product Management have?

options.text: Desirable, viable, feasible, sustainable
Scalable, secure, stable, simple
Planned, funded, staffed, approved
Fast, cheap, good, complete

questions.explanation: Product Management defines solutions that are desirable, viable, feasible and sustainable. The other sets describe technical qualities or project status, not the balance of customer, business and technical fit.

questions.prompt: A team writes a short profile of 'Dana, a night-shift nurse who orders supplies on a phone' to guide its design. Which tool is this?

options.text: A benefit hypothesis
A persona
A story map
A portfolio canvas

questions.explanation: A persona is a representative characterisation of a user. A story map arranges user activities and stories; it shows what users do, not who they are.

questions.prompt: Design thinking alternates between divergent and convergent thinking. What does that mean in practice?

options.text: Build one solution, then defend it against criticism
Collect requirements first, then freeze them for delivery
Split the team in two and merge the results at the end
Explore many possibilities, then narrow to the best choice

questions.explanation: Divergence widens the range of problems or solutions considered, and convergence narrows it to a choice. Collecting and freezing requirements is the waterfall pattern that design thinking is contrasted with.

questions.prompt: What does the ART backlog hold?

options.text: Epics awaiting portfolio approval
Features and enablers for the train
Defects reported by customers alone
Stories and tasks for one team

questions.explanation: The ART backlog holds the features and enablers that enhance the solution and extend its architectural runway. Epics sit in the portfolio backlog and stories in team backlogs, one level up and one level down.

questions.prompt: Who is responsible for prioritising the features in the ART backlog?

options.text: The Release Train Engineer
The Product Owners by majority vote
The Business Owners' line managers
Product Management

questions.explanation: Product Management manages and prioritises the ART backlog. The Release Train Engineer is the common wrong answer: the RTE facilitates the train and its events and does not own the content.

questions.prompt: Who defines the enablers that prepare a train's technical foundation for future features?

options.text: The System Architect
Product Management alone
The Epic Owner
The Scrum Master/Team Coach

questions.explanation: Product Management defines features, and the System Architect defines enablers. The Epic Owner works at the portfolio level, shepherding epics, and does not define a train's enablers.

questions.prompt: How large is a feature in SAFe?

options.text: Small enough for one ART to deliver within a PI
Large enough to span several trains in a Solution Train
Large enough to need several PIs and a business case
Small enough for one team to finish in an iteration

questions.explanation: A feature is sized to be delivered by a single ART within one PI. Work that fits in an iteration is a story, and work that spans several PIs with a business case is an epic.

questions.prompt: Besides a name, what does a well-formed feature include?

options.text: A task breakdown and hour estimates
A project charter and a risk register
A Lean business case and an MVP definition
A benefit hypothesis and acceptance criteria

questions.explanation: A feature carries a benefit hypothesis and acceptance criteria. A Lean business case and an MVP belong to epics, which is the confusion this question tests.

questions.prompt: How does SAFe calculate Weighted Shortest Job First?

options.text: Business value multiplied by the size of the job
Cost of Delay added to the risk exposure
Job size divided by the velocity of the team
Cost of Delay divided by job duration or size

questions.explanation: WSJF is the relative Cost of Delay divided by the relative job duration, for which job size is used as a proxy. Multiplying value by size would favour the largest jobs, the opposite of the intent.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a component of Cost of Delay in WSJF?

options.text: Sunk cost to date
Stakeholder seniority
Team velocity
Time criticality

questions.explanation: Cost of Delay combines user-business value, time criticality and risk reduction or opportunity enablement. Sunk cost is explicitly ignored, and seniority of the requester has no place in the calculation.

questions.prompt: Four features have these relative scores. Ash: Cost of Delay 16, size 8. Elm: Cost of Delay 9, size 3. Oak: Cost of Delay 20, size 20. Yew: Cost of Delay 12, size 8. Which should be done first according to WSJF?

options.text: Elm
Oak
Ash
Yew

questions.explanation: WSJF is Cost of Delay divided by size: Elm scores 3, Ash 2, Yew 1.5 and Oak 1, so Elm goes first. Oak has the highest Cost of Delay, which makes it tempting, but its size gives it the lowest score.

questions.prompt: A feature has already consumed two PIs of effort, and a stakeholder argues that it must be finished first for that reason. How does WSJF treat this?

options.text: Money already spent is added to the Cost of Delay of the feature in question
Features that have been started are automatically ranked first
The feature is removed from the backlog and written off
Money already spent is ignored; only remaining work and Cost of Delay count

questions.explanation: WSJF ignores sunk costs and looks at the remaining job size against the Cost of Delay. Finishing what has been started feels right, but past spending does not change which job gives the best return now.

questions.prompt: Stakeholders ask for the Cost of Delay of each feature in dollars before any prioritisation can happen. What does SAFe recommend?

options.text: Estimate the items relative to one another
Ask each stakeholder to rank by importance
Wait until finance has calculated exact values
Use the cost of the development team per PI

questions.explanation: SAFe estimates WSJF with relative values, comparing jobs with each other instead of calculating absolute money figures. Waiting for exact numbers delays the decision the technique is meant to speed up.

questions.prompt: A train keeps postponing enablers and technical debt because features always score higher. Which SAFe mechanism addresses this?

options.text: A separate hardening PI each year
Capacity allocation by type of work
A dedicated technical debt team
A higher WSJF score for all enablers

questions.explanation: Capacity allocation reserves a share of capacity for each work type for the coming planning period, so enablers do not compete head to head with features. A hardening PI is the trap: it lets problems pile up instead of building quality in continuously.

questions.prompt: Where do nonfunctional requirements such as security and performance apply in SAFe?

options.text: As tasks for the final iteration of the PI
As constraints on the design across the backlogs
As acceptance criteria of a single story
As features placed at the bottom of the backlog

questions.explanation: Nonfunctional requirements are system qualities that guide design and act as constraints on the backlogs. Treating them as low-priority backlog items means they are tested late or not at all.

questions.prompt: What is the standard format of PI Planning?

options.text: A one-week workshop for managers, held once a year
A half-day meeting of the team leads at the start of each month
A two-hour session for each team at the start of every iteration
A two-day event for the whole ART, every 8 to 12 weeks

questions.explanation: PI Planning is typically a two-day, cadence-based event for the entire ART, held every 8 to 12 weeks. A per-team session each iteration is iteration planning, a different event.

questions.prompt: Who facilitates PI Planning?

options.text: The Release Train Engineer
The senior Business Owner
The Product Manager
The System Architect

questions.explanation: The Release Train Engineer leads and facilitates PI Planning. Product Management presents the vision and the backlog there, which is why it is the tempting wrong answer.

questions.prompt: Which are the two primary outputs of PI Planning?

options.text: A detailed Gantt chart and a resource plan
Committed PI objectives and the ART planning board
A release planning calendar and a signed scope statement
An approved business case and a budget

questions.explanation: PI Planning produces committed PI objectives from the teams and an ART planning board. A Gantt chart and a resource plan are the project-management equivalents that SAFe does not produce.

questions.prompt: What does the ART planning board show?

options.text: Individual task assignments and the hours remaining
Defect counts and test coverage for each team
Feature delivery dates and dependencies between teams
Budget spent and forecast spend per value stream

questions.explanation: The ART planning board shows when features are expected and the dependencies among teams. It is not a task board; task detail stays with each team.

questions.prompt: Who assigns business value to the teams' PI objectives during PI Planning?

options.text: Product Owners
Business Owners
The Release Train Engineer
Business analysts on each team

questions.explanation: Business Owners assign business value, on a scale from 1 to 10, to each team's PI objectives in a conversation with the team. Product Owners help write the objectives, but they do not score them.

questions.prompt: A team's objective depends on a vendor delivery that may not arrive in time. How should the team treat it in its PI plan?

options.text: As an uncommitted objective
As a stretch goal for the IP iteration
As a committed objective with extra overtime
As a risk to leave out of the plan

questions.explanation: PI objectives are either committed or uncommitted, and uncommitted objectives cover work with significant uncertainty. The work is still planned; it is simply excluded from the commitment so that predictability stays honest.

questions.prompt: In the confidence vote at the end of PI Planning, the average vote across the train is two fingers out of five. What should happen?

options.text: The low votes are recorded and the event closes on time
The teams that voted low are asked to vote again in private
The plans are reworked until the teams can commit
The managers adjust the plans after the event has ended

questions.explanation: A low confidence vote means the plan is not yet a commitment, so the concerns are addressed and the plan is reworked. Managers fixing the plan afterwards is the trap: the people who do the work must own the plan.

questions.prompt: What do the letters ROAM stand for when risks are addressed in PI Planning?

options.text: Reported, Owned, Avoided, Measured
Reviewed, Ordered, Assigned, Monitored
Resolved, Owned, Accepted, Mitigated
Raised, Open, Active, Managed

questions.explanation: ART risks are categorised as Resolved, Owned, Accepted or Mitigated. Owned and Accepted are the two most often mixed up: an owned risk has a person responsible, an accepted risk is understood and left as it is.

questions.prompt: During PI Planning a risk cannot be resolved in the room, and a director agrees to take responsibility for it afterwards. Which ROAM category applies?

options.text: Accepted
Mitigated
Owned
Resolved

questions.explanation: A risk that someone takes responsibility for after the event is Owned. Mitigated would require a plan that has already been identified to reduce the risk's impact.

questions.prompt: At the end of the first day of PI Planning, the draft plans show the train is overloaded. What happens next in the standard agenda?

options.text: The teams are told to raise their capacity estimates to fit the features
The overloaded features are moved into the IP iteration without discussion
A management review and problem-solving session adjusts scope or resources
The Release Train Engineer extends the Planning Interval by one iteration

questions.explanation: Day one ends with a management review and problem-solving meeting, where leaders make the adjustments the draft plans call for, and teams replan on day two. Inflating capacity estimates hides the problem and destroys the commitment.

questions.prompt: Who typically presents the product vision and the top features at PI Planning?

options.text: The Lean-Agile Center of Excellence
The Product Owners as a group
Product Management
The Scrum Masters/Team Coaches

questions.explanation: Product Management leads the vision and roadmap and presents the vision and the highest-priority features. Business Owners or senior leaders present the business context, a separate briefing.

questions.prompt: Which three areas of readiness does an ART prepare before PI Planning?

options.text: Design sign-off, build setup and test readiness
Legal review, security review and audit readiness
Organizational, content and logistics readiness
Budget approval, staffing levels and tooling readiness

questions.explanation: Preparation covers organisational readiness, content readiness and logistics readiness. Content readiness is the one most often neglected: a vision and a prioritised backlog must exist before the event.

questions.prompt: To save cost, a director proposes that only the team leads attend PI Planning and brief their teams afterwards. What is SAFe's view?

options.text: The Business Owners should attend in place of the teams
The proposal is fine for trains with more than eight teams
The whole ART plans together, since those who do the work own the plan
The proposal is fine, provided the leads take detailed notes and share them

questions.explanation: PI Planning is for the entire ART, because alignment, dependency discovery and commitment come from everyone planning together. A plan relayed by team leads is a plan that the teams never committed to.

questions.prompt: What is the most common structure of a Planning Interval?

options.text: Two development iterations followed by two test iterations
One planning iteration followed by ten development iterations
Four or five development iterations followed by one IP iteration
Three hardening iterations followed by a release weekend

questions.explanation: A PI typically runs 8 to 12 weeks, most often as four or five development iterations and one Innovation and Planning iteration. SAFe has no hardening or test-only iterations.

questions.prompt: A Product Manager wants to schedule two features into the Innovation and Planning iteration to raise throughput. What is SAFe's guidance?

options.text: The IP iteration is reserved for defect fixing
No feature work is planned into the IP iteration
Features may be planned there if the teams agree
The IP iteration should carry the largest features

questions.explanation: During PI Planning no work is planned into the IP iteration, which provides an estimating buffer and time for innovation, learning, PI Planning and Inspect and Adapt. It is also not a defect-fixing iteration.

questions.prompt: What is the likely effect of regularly filling the IP iteration with planned feature work?

options.text: Teams become better at estimating their capacity
Predictability improves because more of the capacity is planned
PI objectives are missed more often and innovation time disappears
The next PI Planning becomes shorter and easier to run

questions.explanation: The IP iteration acts as an estimating buffer for meeting PI objectives and as time for innovation and learning. Removing the buffer makes every estimation error visible as a missed objective.

questions.prompt: What does the System Demo show?

options.text: The stories of one team, reviewed by that team's own stakeholders and users
A slide presentation of status and planned work for the next PI
The finished solution, once at the end of each release
The integrated work of all teams on the train from the latest iteration

questions.explanation: The System Demo gives an integrated view of the new features from all teams on the ART for the most recent iteration. One team showing its own stories is the Iteration Review.

questions.prompt: Each team on a train shows its own stories to its own stakeholders every iteration, and nothing is shown integrated until the end of the PI. What is missing?

options.text: The Coach Sync during each iteration
The System Demo after each iteration
The Strategic Portfolio Review each quarter
The Iteration Retrospective of each team

questions.explanation: The Iteration Review covers one team, while the System Demo shows the integrated increment of the whole train at the end of each iteration, in a production-like environment. Without it, integration problems stay hidden for the whole PI.

questions.prompt: Arrange the three parts of the Inspect and Adapt event in order.

options.text: Retrospective and problem-solving workshop
Quantitative and qualitative measurement
PI System Demo

questions.explanation: Inspect and Adapt starts with the PI System Demo, continues with the measurement review and ends with the retrospective and problem-solving workshop. The demo comes first, because the measurements and the workshop build on what was actually delivered.

questions.prompt: What happens to the improvement items identified in the problem-solving workshop?

options.text: They are sent to the PMO for approval and funding
They are stored in the retrospective notes for reference
They are assigned to the Release Train Engineer to complete
They enter the ART backlog for the next PI Planning

questions.explanation: Improvement items go into the ART backlog and are planned into upcoming PIs, with the ART owning the actions. Giving them all to the RTE is the trap: the train, not one role, owns its improvement.

questions.prompt: Match each ART event to its purpose.

options.text: Evaluating the solution and identifying improvements at the end of the PI
Reviewing progress toward PI objectives and adjusting scope where needed
Coordinating dependencies and raising impediments
Approving the budget for each value stream
An integrated view of new features from all teams

questions.explanation: The PO Sync tracks progress toward PI objectives, the Coach Sync coordinates dependencies and impediments, the System Demo shows integrated work and Inspect and Adapt closes the PI. The ART Sync combines the PO Sync and the Coach Sync.

questions.prompt: How is ART predictability assessed?

options.text: By measuring the hours worked against the hours that were originally estimated
By tracking how many features were started during the PI
By comparing the business value achieved with the business value planned
By counting the story points completed by each team per iteration

questions.explanation: The ART Predictability Measure compares the actual business value achieved for PI objectives with the planned value. Story points measure a team's output and cannot be compared or summed across teams as a measure of predictability.

questions.prompt: A train plans in 10-week PIs, and a stakeholder concludes that customers can receive new functionality only every 10 weeks. What is wrong with this conclusion?

options.text: Releases happen every iteration, never at PI boundaries
The PI length must be shortened to release more often
Customers receive functionality once a year in SAFe
Planning cadence and release timing are separate in SAFe

questions.explanation: SAFe plans on cadence and releases on demand, so a release can happen whenever the business needs it. Shortening the PI treats the planning rhythm as the release schedule, which is the same mistake.

questions.prompt: What does Lean Portfolio Management do?

options.text: Assigns people to projects according to their utilisation
Aligns strategy and execution using Lean and systems thinking
Tracks project budgets and reports variances each month
Approves the detailed requirements of every feature

questions.explanation: LPM aligns strategy and execution by applying Lean and systems thinking to strategy and investment funding, Agile portfolio operations and governance. Tracking project variances is traditional portfolio management, which LPM replaces.

questions.prompt: Which three areas does Lean Portfolio Management cover?

options.text: Strategy and investment funding, Agile portfolio operations, Lean governance
Continuous Exploration, Continuous Integration, Continuous Deployment
Scope management, schedule management, cost management and quality management
Team backlogs, ART backlogs, portfolio backlogs and Solution Train backlogs

questions.explanation: LPM covers strategy and investment funding, Agile portfolio operations and Lean governance. Scope, schedule and cost are the project-management triple constraint, the frame LPM moves away from.

questions.prompt: How does SAFe define a portfolio?

options.text: A set of value streams that deliver solutions within common funding and governance
A group of applications that is maintained by one IT department
A collection of teams that report to the same vice president
A list of approved projects with their budgets, owners and delivery deadlines

questions.explanation: A SAFe portfolio is a set of value streams delivering solutions under common funding and governance. A list of projects is the traditional definition and the one the exam expects you to reject.

questions.prompt: At Tessel Bank, staff take a mortgage from application to payout, and three trains build the software those staff use. How does SAFe classify the two?

options.text: The mortgage process is a development value stream; the trains form an operational value stream
Both are operational value streams, since both serve the bank's customers
Both are development value streams, since both depend on software
The mortgage process is an operational value stream; the trains form a development value stream

questions.explanation: An operational value stream delivers the product or service to the customer, and a development value stream builds the solutions that make it possible. Reversing the two is the usual error.

questions.prompt: How are development and operational value streams related?

options.text: Operational value streams fund and staff the development ones
The two are independent of each other and are managed in separate portfolios
Development value streams build the solutions that operational ones use
Development value streams replace operational ones over time

questions.explanation: Development value streams build and maintain the solutions that operational value streams use to serve customers. They are connected, which is why operational streams are identified first when trains are designed.

questions.prompt: What does a development value stream consist of?

options.text: One project and its steering committee
One or more Agile Release Trains
A set of functional departments
A single cross-functional Agile Team

questions.explanation: Each development value stream consists of one or more ARTs. A single team is too small to be a value stream, and functional departments are the structure value streams cut across.

questions.prompt: What are Strategic Themes?

options.text: Marketing messages that describe the strategic roadmap
Epics that the portfolio has approved for the current year
Topics for the next Inspect and Adapt problem-solving workshop agenda
Portfolio-level business objectives tied to enterprise strategy

questions.explanation: Strategic Themes are portfolio-level business objectives that give competitive differentiation and connect the portfolio to the enterprise strategy. They are not epics; they are the context in which epics are judged.

questions.prompt: In which format does SAFe recommend stating Strategic Themes?

options.text: User stories with acceptance criteria
Objectives and Key Results
A Lean business case
A SWOT quadrant

questions.explanation: Strategic Themes are best stated as OKRs, in plain business language, so progress can be measured. A Lean business case belongs to an epic.

questions.prompt: Epic Owners at Quarry Insurance propose epics that have no connection to any Strategic Theme. What role should the themes play?

options.text: They are informational and do not affect epic decisions
They are rewritten each PI to match the epics chosen
They apply to teams but not to the portfolio backlog
They provide the business context for portfolio decisions

questions.explanation: Strategic Themes give the business context for portfolio strategy and decisions, and trains refer to them when defining epics and features. Rewriting themes to fit the epics turns the strategy upside down.

questions.prompt: Which question should an enterprise strategy answer, according to SAFe?

options.text: Which defects are fixed first?
Which developer joins which team?
Which customers and markets do we serve?
Which stories fit into the next iteration?

questions.explanation: The enterprise strategy answers which customers and markets are served, which products and solutions are provided, what unique value and resources are brought, and how these will be extended. The other questions are team-level decisions.

questions.prompt: What does the Portfolio Vision describe?

options.text: The current organisation chart of the portfolio's departments
The approved budget of the portfolio for the financial year
The detailed release plan of every train in the portfolio
The future state of the portfolio's value streams and solutions

questions.explanation: The Portfolio Vision describes the future state of the portfolio's value streams and solutions and is a key input for identifying epics. It is aspirational yet achievable, not a budget or a release plan.

questions.prompt: Leaders want one page that captures the portfolio's value streams, solutions, customers and revenue streams. Which SAFe tool is this?

options.text: The ART planning board
The portfolio Kanban board
The portfolio canvas
The epic hypothesis statement

questions.explanation: The portfolio canvas defines a portfolio's development value streams, solutions, revenue streams, customers and other key elements. The Lean business case describes one epic, not the whole portfolio.

questions.prompt: A portfolio has completed a SWOT analysis and now wants to derive strategic options for its future state from it. Which technique does SAFe use?

options.text: Value stream mapping
Pareto analysis
WSJF scoring
TOWS analysis

questions.explanation: TOWS takes the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats from a SWOT analysis and combines them into strategic options. Pareto analysis is used in the problem-solving workshop to select the biggest root cause.

questions.prompt: What does the portfolio backlog hold?

options.text: Business and enabler epics
Stories and defects for one team
Features and enablers for one train
Strategic themes and OKRs

questions.explanation: The portfolio backlog is a Kanban system for business and enabler epics. Features and enablers for a train sit one level down, in the ART backlog.

questions.prompt: Arrange the states of the portfolio Kanban in order.

options.text: Analyzing
Implementing
Funnel
Ready
Reviewing
Done

questions.explanation: Epics enter the funnel, are reviewed, analysed, made ready, implemented and finished. Reviewing comes before Analyzing: an idea is first shaped into an epic hypothesis and only then given the deeper analysis.

questions.prompt: In which state of the portfolio Kanban is the Lean business case developed and the MVP defined?

options.text: Analyzing
Funnel
Done
Implementing

questions.explanation: The Analyzing state is where the Lean business case and the MVP are worked out, leading to a go or no-go decision. The funnel only captures ideas, with no analysis effort yet.

questions.prompt: A portfolio proposes moving its services to a new cloud platform to support future business needs, with no direct customer feature. What kind of epic is this?

options.text: A business epic
An enabler epic
A capability
A strategic theme

questions.explanation: Enabler epics extend the architectural runway for future business or technical needs, while business epics deliver value directly to customers. A capability is large-solution functionality, a different level.

questions.prompt: A sponsor says an approved epic is 'just a project with a new name'. Which statement reflects SAFe?

options.text: An epic is closed when its planned scope is delivered, whatever the outcome
An epic needs an MVP and a Lean business case and is managed through the portfolio Kanban
An epic has a fixed scope, a fixed budget and a named project manager who is accountable
An epic is a financial allocation that teams draw down as they complete tasks

questions.explanation: SAFe states that an epic is not a project: it needs an MVP and a Lean business case and flows through the portfolio Kanban. Fixed scope and a project manager describe the model that epics replace.

questions.prompt: What does an Epic Owner do?

options.text: Prioritises the backlog of one Agile Team
Approves the budget of the whole portfolio each year
Facilitates the PI Planning event for a train
Coordinates an epic through the portfolio Kanban

questions.explanation: The Epic Owner coordinates the progress of an epic through the portfolio Kanban. The Epic Owner does not approve the epic or the budget; that is Portfolio Leadership's role.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the MVP for an epic?

options.text: To demonstrate the team's velocity to the sponsor
To satisfy the audit requirement for a prototype
To prove or disprove the epic's hypothesis early
To deliver the first release of the full planned scope

questions.explanation: An MVP is an early, minimal version of a solution used to prove or disprove the epic hypothesis. It is not the first slice of a fixed scope; its job is learning.

questions.prompt: An epic's MVP shows that customers do not value the idea, but the sponsor argues the full scope must be built because the epic was approved. What does SAFe expect?

options.text: Completion of the scope, since approval is a commitment
A pivot or stop decision based on the evidence
A change of Epic Owner to restore confidence
A larger MVP, built before any decision is taken

questions.explanation: The Lean Startup cycle ends in a pivot-or-persevere decision driven by the MVP's evidence. Approval to implement is approval to test a hypothesis, not a commitment to deliver the whole scope.

questions.prompt: Who approves epics for implementation?

options.text: The Product Owners
Portfolio Leadership
The Epic Owner
The Release Train Engineer

questions.explanation: Because of their scope, epics must be approved by Portfolio Leadership, the term the current framework pages use; older material names Lean Portfolio Management. The Epic Owner is the tempting answer, but that role shepherds the epic and prepares the case; it does not approve its own epic.

questions.prompt: Which role establishes the technology vision, strategy and roadmap for a portfolio?

options.text: Product Manager
Release Train Engineer
System Architect
Enterprise Architect

questions.explanation: The Enterprise Architect sets the portfolio's technology vision, strategy and roadmap. The System Architect does similar work for a single train, which is why the two are confused.

questions.prompt: What do Lean Budgets fund?

options.text: Functional departments
Individual projects
Named features
Value streams

questions.explanation: Lean Budgets fund value streams instead of projects. Funding projects is the practice SAFe identifies as a blocker to agility.

questions.prompt: At Larkspur Logistics every new initiative needs its own cost approval, and people are reassigned between projects several times a year. What does SAFe recommend?

options.text: Approve projects faster through a weekly funding committee meeting
Fund long-lived value streams and bring the work to them
Merge small projects into fewer, larger programmes
Give each project a dedicated cost controller

questions.explanation: Lean Budgets fund value streams with stable teams, which removes the overhead of project cost accounting and repeated approvals. A faster committee keeps the project model and only shortens one of its queues.

questions.prompt: A value stream has an approved budget, and a feature takes longer than expected. What happens under Lean Budgets?

options.text: A change request is raised for additional project funding
The feature is cancelled because it exceeded its estimate
The budget is recalculated and approved again by finance
The budget stays the same and priorities are adjusted locally

questions.explanation: With value stream funding, content decisions and trade-offs are made locally within the budget, so an overrun on one feature needs no re-approval. A change request is the project-accounting reflex this model removes.

questions.prompt: Match each Lean budget guardrail to what it balances or ensures.

options.text: Ongoing business involvement in priorities
Sign-off of each story before work starts
The mix of new features, enablers and maintenance
Spending across near-term and longer-term solutions
Portfolio review of large epics

questions.explanation: The four guardrails are investment horizons, capacity allocation, approval of significant initiatives and continuous Business Owner engagement. The first two are quantitative, and the last two are about how the budget is governed.

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of the four Lean budget guardrails?

options.text: Continuous Business Owner engagement
Monthly project status reporting
Annual zero-based budgeting
Fixed scope per Planning Interval

questions.explanation: Continuous Business Owner engagement is one of the four guardrails. Status reporting and fixed scope are project controls, which the guardrails replace with lighter governance.

questions.prompt: In SAFe's investment horizons, which horizon covers solutions that are being retired?

options.text: Horizon 1
Horizon 3
Horizon 2
Horizon 0

questions.explanation: Horizon 0 covers solutions being decommissioned, while Horizon 1 covers solutions that deliver value today. Horizon 3 is at the other end: early evaluation of future opportunities.

questions.prompt: A value stream has its own budget and wants to start a very large initiative that exceeds the portfolio's epic threshold. What applies?

options.text: The portfolio is informed after the work has started
The initiative is split into stories to avoid review
The Release Train Engineer decides at PI Planning
The initiative needs portfolio approval as an epic

questions.explanation: The guardrail on approving significant initiatives requires large initiatives to go through portfolio review, even when a value stream is funded. Value stream budgets give local freedom over content, not over portfolio-sized bets.

questions.prompt: How often is the Strategic Portfolio Review typically held?

options.text: Each iteration, before iteration planning
Quarterly, at least a month before the next PI Planning
Weekly, on the day after each System Demo has been held
Annually, as part of the budgeting cycle

questions.explanation: The Strategic Portfolio Review is typically quarterly and is held at least one month before the next PI Planning, so its decisions can shape the backlog. An annual review is the traditional cycle that is too slow to steer by.

questions.prompt: How often is the Portfolio Sync generally held?

options.text: Each iteration
Twice a year
Daily
Monthly

questions.explanation: The Portfolio Sync is generally a monthly event with an operational focus. In a month when the Strategic Portfolio Review takes place, that review may replace it.

questions.prompt: Portfolio stakeholders meet to decide together how the portfolio's funds are divided among value streams. Which LPM event is this?

options.text: Inspect and Adapt
PI Planning
The Portfolio Sync
Participatory budgeting

questions.explanation: Participatory budgeting is the collaborative event in which stakeholders allocate the portfolio budget to value streams; the current glossary also calls it Strategic Investment Planning. The Portfolio Sync reviews operations and does not set the budgets.

questions.prompt: A company adopting SAFe asks what becomes of its Project Management Office. What does SAFe suggest?

options.text: It continues unchanged and approves each train's plans
It becomes the management office for all Release Train Engineers
It can evolve into a Value Management Office that supports LPM
It is closed, and its staff are assigned to Agile Teams

questions.explanation: The Value Management Office supports Lean Portfolio Management with governance and operations, and a PMO's skills are often redirected there. Closing the PMO outright throws away knowledge the portfolio still needs.

questions.prompt: How does SAFe describe Lean-Agile Leadership?

options.text: Leaders step back and let teams define the strategy
Leaders drive and sustain change by empowering individuals and teams
Leaders delegate the transformation to certified coaches
Leaders set detailed plans and check each week that all the teams follow them

questions.explanation: Lean-Agile Leadership describes how leaders drive and sustain organisational change and operational excellence by empowering individuals and teams to reach their potential. Delegating the change is the tempting answer and the one SAFe rejects.

questions.prompt: Teams at Pinecrest Telecom work in an Agile way, but annual budgeting, performance reviews and approval boards are unchanged, and nobody below the executives can alter them. What does this illustrate?

options.text: That the Release Train Engineer should redesign the policies
That SAFe is unsuitable for a company of this size
That only leaders can change the system in which people work
That teams need more Agile training before SAFe can work

questions.explanation: SAFe holds that only managers, executives and other leaders can change the systems that govern how work is done. More team training cannot fix policies the teams have no authority over.

questions.prompt: A director asks teams for full transparency about problems, yet never admits to mistakes of their own. Which leadership behaviour is missing?

options.text: Applying cadence
Leading by example
Decentralising decisions
Taking an economic view

questions.explanation: Leaders lead by example, modelling the mindset, values and behaviours they ask of others. People copy what leaders do far more than what leaders say.

questions.prompt: What is the first step of the SAFe Implementation Roadmap?

options.text: Create the Implementation Plan
Reaching the Tipping Point
Train Teams and Launch ART
Organize Around Value

questions.explanation: The roadmap begins with Reaching the Tipping Point, where the need for change overcomes resistance to it. Launching a train is the visible step, but it comes much later in the sequence.

questions.prompt: Arrange these steps of the SAFe Implementation Roadmap in order.

options.text: Train Lean-Agile Change Agents
Organize Around Value
Train Teams and Launch ART
Coach ART Execution
Create the Implementation Plan
Reaching the Tipping Point

questions.explanation: The roadmap moves from the tipping point through training change agents and leaders, organising around value and planning, to launching and coaching the first train. Organising around value comes before the implementation plan, since the plan needs to know which value streams and trains exist.

questions.prompt: A profitable company faces no crisis, but its executives foresee disruption and set out a compelling vision for change. Which route to the tipping point is this?

options.text: A grassroots movement
A regulatory mandate
Proactive leadership
A burning platform

questions.explanation: SAFe names two routes to the tipping point: a burning platform, where failure to compete is obvious, and visionary leaders who act before a crisis. With no crisis in sight, this is the proactive route.

questions.prompt: Which three benefits does a vision for change provide?

options.text: Authority, control and compliance
Scope, schedule and budget
Speed, savings and headcount
Purpose, motivation and alignment

questions.explanation: A vision for change gives purpose, motivation and alignment. Scope, schedule and budget belong to a project plan, not to a vision.

questions.prompt: One enthusiastic Agile coach is trying to drive a SAFe transformation across three business units without executive involvement. What does SAFe say is needed?

options.text: A stricter rollout schedule
A new tool for tracking adoption
A sufficiently powerful guiding coalition
A larger budget for external coaching days

questions.explanation: A vision is not enough; a powerful guiding coalition of influential leaders is needed to carry the change. A single coach lacks the authority to change the system, however capable.

questions.prompt: Which group is a small Agile team dedicated to implementing the SAFe way of working?

options.text: The Lean-Agile Center of Excellence
The System Team
The Agile Program Management Office
The Value Management Office

questions.explanation: The Lean-Agile Center of Excellence is a small Agile team that implements the Lean-Agile way of working. The Value Management Office supports portfolio governance, a different job.

questions.prompt: Whose work on change management does the SAFe Implementation Roadmap draw on?

options.text: Frederick Taylor
Henry Gantt
Michael Porter
John Kotter

questions.explanation: The roadmap's strategy is sourced partly from John Kotter's change management work, including the guiding coalition and short-term wins. Taylor and Gantt represent the scientific management tradition that Lean-Agile thinking moves away from.

questions.prompt: An AI assistant analyses a train's flow metrics and recommends disbanding one team. What is the leader's responsibility?

options.text: Evaluate the recommendation and remain accountable for the decision
Ask the assistant to announce the decision to the team
Ignore the output, since AI cannot understand teams
Carry out the recommendation, since it comes straight from the data

questions.explanation: The course emphasises human-in-the-loop evaluation, so the leader checks the analysis and owns the decision. Following the output because it is data-driven hands accountability to a tool.

questions.prompt: Which use of AI by a leader fits SAFe's guidance?

options.text: Letting an assistant decide which epics are approved
Pasting confidential salary data into a public chatbot for analysis
Replacing the System Demo with generated status text
Summarising Inspect and Adapt findings as input to a decision

questions.explanation: AI supports leaders by preparing and summarising information, while people evaluate the output and decide. Replacing the System Demo with generated text removes the objective evidence of a working system.

notes.back: Quality practices run throughout development; quality is not inspected in at the end.

notes.front: What is the WSJF formula?
notes.back: Cost of Delay divided by job duration (job size).
notes.explanation: Highest WSJF goes first. Sunk cost is ignored.

notes.back: Two days, the whole ART, every 8 to 12 weeks, facilitated by the RTE.
notes.explanation: Outputs: committed PI objectives and the ART planning board.

notes.back: Business Owners, on a scale of 1 to 10.
notes.explanation: Not the Product Owners. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: What is an uncommitted PI objective?
notes.back: Planned work with significant uncertainty that is left out of the commitment.
notes.explanation: It keeps the commitment reliable.

notes.front: What is the Innovation and Planning iteration for?
notes.back: An estimating buffer, plus innovation, learning, PI Planning and Inspect and Adapt.
notes.explanation: No feature work is planned into it.

notes.front: What is the System Demo?
notes.back: An integrated view of new features from all teams, at the end of each iteration.

notes.front: What is a SAFe portfolio?
notes.back: A set of value streams that deliver solutions within common funding and governance.
notes.explanation: Not a list of projects.

notes.front: Operational or development value stream: which one builds the solutions?
notes.back: The development value stream. The operational one delivers the service to the customer.
notes.explanation: Distractors often reverse them.

notes.front: What are Strategic Themes, and how are they written?
notes.back: Portfolio-level business objectives linking the portfolio to enterprise strategy, written as OKRs.
notes.explanation: They give the context for epic decisions.

notes.back: A Lean business case, an MVP and approval by Portfolio Leadership.
